newsitem.title: USA: Hard-boiled lessons in becoming self-employed.
newsitem.headline: Hard-boiled lessons in becoming self-employed.

text.p: You might have thought about becoming self-employed and even talked to friends about quitting your job and taking the leap. But what do you actually need to do to get the business running and make it work?

It's a fair question, one that often comes after reading all the motivational material crowding the business bookshelves and ploughing through the ones about starting companies -- which is not actually about being self-employed.

Linda Stern, a personal finance columnist, tried to answer the question by boiling down the articles she wrote for Home Office Computing magazine and considering all the things she has done -- successful and not -- in running her own freelance business for the past decade.
Her book, "Money Smart Secrets for the Self-Employed," was recently published by Random House.

"There's a million-and-one money books out there but there's not really a money book for people who work for themselves," Stern, who is also a longtime personal finance columnist for Reuters, said in an interview.
This is not a book about the spiritual fulfilment of self-employment, or a primer on the emotional anxieties of leaving a steady paycheck.

What it does offer are the nitty gritty lessons in getting a business running -- how to set up a cash flow spreadsheet, figure out what to charge for your services, determine whether to lease or buy a computer, or evaluate whether it pays to put your kids and spouse on the payroll, among other things.
"When I quit my job I didn't do a lot of the things I recommend you do in this book," Stern said. "A lot of it emerged from talking with other people and just doing it as I went along."
She also points out that as a writer, she learned about personal finance by talking to experts in the field -- lessons that not only went into her stories but into her business.

The book begins with chapters on record keeping, taxes and figuring out how much you need to survive. To do that, Stern offers sample spreadsheets that any self-employed person could use, and discusses personal finance software.

"Everybody makes common mistakes when starting out and one that's almost a mythology is that if you work at home the IRS is going to get you. The biggest mistake people make starting out is that they don't take enough deductions," she said.

Other common problems include -- penny pinching on things that matter, like failing to install a dedicated fax or computer modem line to free up your other line for phone calls, or spending too much on non-essentials like office furnishings or plants and paintings to impress clients.

One of the most valuable lessons in the book is figuring out how much to charge, a common problem for self-employed people who often don't charge enough or fail to steer their business to clients who pay well.

Rather than picking a figure out of the air, Stern offers a spreadsheet in which you work backward from your annual goal -- which includes business costs and taxes and is correlated with your household budget -- to figure out an hourly rate you need to make. Then she tells you how to get it.
She also discusses loans, hiring help, health insurance and retirement planning -- all the practical problems that come with running your own business.

Stern is convinced that you can make more money working for yourself than as an employee, for you get to take a salary and keep any business profits as well. It may not happen right away, but the diligent do get there.

She makes another point about self-employment, especially pertinent in these times of healthy economic growth but continued corporate downsizing. Self-employment is often viewed as a risky enterprise. But Stern points out that it may be far more foolhardy to depend on your employer for your financial future.
"People who aren't thinking about these things, I think that's riskier than working for yourself," she said.
